vignette:
**Patient Vignette: "Marta"**

Marta is a 60-year-old midwife who has worked in the same community hospital for thirty-four years. She has been with her partner, a retired carpenter, for twenty-two years. She presents as a sturdy, capable woman whose hands are never still—she twists a tissue, smooths her skirt, adjusts the clasp on her watch. She speaks in a low, measured voice, as if she is trying to keep herself from shouting.

The event happened fourteen months ago, on a Tuesday in late September. Marta was assisting with a complicated delivery. The patient, a young woman with preeclampsia, had begun to hemorrhage. Marta remembers the room: the bright lights, the fetal monitor beeping, the obstetrician’s calm instructions. She remembers reaching for a sterile solution on a high shelf. The bottle was old, the seal cracked. When she tipped it to pour, a thick, acrid liquid splashed onto her left forearm and splattered across her face. It was not saline. It was a chemical disinfectant that had been mislabeled and left in the supply room for years.

At first, there was no pain. Then her skin began to burn. She finished the delivery—the baby was healthy, the mother stabilized—and then she walked to the emergency sink. Her forearm was already blistering. Her eyes were red, streaming. The smell of the chemical stayed in her nose for three days.

She was treated at the hospital’s burn unit. The physical wounds healed in six weeks. But something else did not. In the months that followed, Marta began to notice that her body felt wrong. Her skin, especially on her left arm, was hypersensitive. The touch of clothing, a breeze, her partner’s hand—all of it felt like a scratch. She started wearing long sleeves even in summer. She stopped wearing her watch.

The nightmares began in November. They are not about the chemical. They are about the delivery. In the dream, the patient is bleeding and bleeding, and Marta cannot find the bottle, or the bottle is full of acid, or the baby is drowning in a red tide. She wakes gasping, her heart pounding, her left arm tingling. She does not call out. She lies still until her partner’s breathing tells her it is safe to move.

At work, she has become someone she does not recognize. For thirty years, Marta was the calm in the room—the midwife who could talk a woman through a contraction, who could catch a baby with her eyes closed. Now, she flinches when a colleague opens a cabinet. She avoids the supply room. She has started checking every bottle twice, three times, before she touches it. The other midwives have noticed. They ask if she is tired. She says she is fine.

The most difficult part, Marta says, is the guilt. She was the one who reached for the bottle. She was the one who did not check the label. She knows, intellectually, that the hospital’s inventory system was flawed, that the bottle should never have been there. But at night, in the dark, she replays the moment: her hand reaching up, the seal breaking, the splash. She feels the burn again. She thinks: *If I had been more careful. If I had looked.*

She has stopped going to the grocery store. The cleaning aisle, with its rows of bleach and ammonia, makes her dizzy. She has stopped cooking with vinegar. Her partner does all the shopping now, and when he comes home, he leaves the bags on the porch for her to bring in later. She does not tell him why. She does not want him to see her as fragile.

On the PCL-5, Marta scored a 54. She endorsed severe intrusive thoughts, avoidance of internal and external reminders, negative alterations in cognition and mood, and marked hyperarousal. She does not see herself as a trauma survivor. She sees herself as a woman who made a mistake and is now paying for it. She is angry at herself, at the hospital, at the young mother whose delivery she helped, and at her own body for refusing to forget.

Yesterday, she told me that she used to love the smell of a newborn’s head. Now, when she holds a baby, she smells only chemicals. She is not sure she can go back to deliveries. She is not sure who she is if she cannot.
